programs.name: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain (ACT)
founders: Steven C. Hayes (with Kirk Strosahl, Kelly Wilson)
Lance M. McCracken (pain application)
Kevin E. Vowles (pain application)
JoAnne Dahl (pain application)
Rikard Wicksell (pain application)
programs.founded_year_range: ACT origins early 1980s ('comprehensive distancing'); manual 1999; chronic-pain application ~2004-2005 (Dahl et al. and McCracken books, 2005); Stanza app (Swing Therapeutics) FDA De Novo DEN220083, 9 May 2023
programs.cost_summary: Non-proprietary model, free to use. US clinician delivery is roughly USD 100-250 per session (~USD 800-2,500 for 8-12 sessions out of pocket; typical market range, estimate), usually insurance-covered. Free at point of use in NHS pain services. Self-help books ~USD 15-25. Stanza (Swing Therapeutics) requires a prescription and is offered through clinical partners in 8 US states; its price is not publicly listed.
programs.mechanism_summary: ACT attributes disability and suffering in chronic pain mainly to psychological inflexibility rather than to pain itself. The components are experiential avoidance and control efforts, cognitive fusion with pain-related thoughts, and a narrowing of behaviour away from valued activities. The theory rests on Relational Frame Theory, a behavioural account of language. ACT makes no claim that pain is brain-generated or reversible and no aetiological claims about specific syndromes. The goal is valued living with pain; pain reduction is a by-product. Mediation evidence is mixed: psychological inflexibility mediated outcomes in Wicksell 2013 and Kemani 2016, and acceptance did so in Simister 2018, but 4 of 5 path models showed no mediation in EFFIGACT (Luciano 2014).

programs.name: Alexander Technique
founders: F. Matthias Alexander (1869-1955)
Society of Teachers of the Alexander Technique (STAT, UK, 1958)
AmSAT / Alexander Technique USA (1987)
programs.founded_year_range: 1890s (Alexander developed the method for his own voice loss); taught in London from 1904; first teacher training in 1931; STAT 1958; AmSAT 1987
programs.cost_summary: Independent certified teachers (at least 1,600 h of training over 3 years, per AmSAT). Approx. (unverified) US $60-150 or UK £40-80 per lesson; a typical course of 10-30 lessons costs roughly $1,000-3,000. In trials: £596 for 24 lessons plus exercise (ATEAM, 2008 costing), and an incremental cost of £667 per patient (ATLAS).
programs.mechanism_summary: Pain and dysfunction are attributed to habitual "misuse": unconscious excess muscular effort organised around a disrupted head-neck-back "primary control." This misuse is maintained by unreliable kinaesthetic sense and by "end-gaining." Alexander treated mind and body as one psychophysical unit. Modern neuroscience reframing (Cacciatore and colleagues) presents AT as training adaptive central regulation of axial postural tone and reducing maladaptive co-contraction, with improved body awareness and self-efficacy (the latter associated with outcome in ATLAS). AT does not invoke central sensitisation, limbic, emotional or immune mechanisms. One model is applied to all complaints, and teachers do not diagnose.

programs.mechanism_summary: A physical plus psychological stressor (infection, vaccination, surgery, childbirth, life stress) leaves the ANS stuck in sympathetic "survival mode." Central sensitisation and a conditioned threat response keep it there. This produces secondary dysfunctions (mitochondrial, endocrine, gut, immune or infection, methylation, neurotransmitter), which in turn act as physical triggers that close a vicious loop. The Science page presents ME/CFS (including PVFS and 'adrenal fatigue'), PVFS-type long COVID, fibromyalgia, POTS, MCS, EHS and IBS as one illness. It puts SSD, FND and CRPS on the same spectrum and treats chronic Lyme and mould as secondary infections or triggers.

programs.category: psychological/neuroplastic-pain therapy (nonprofit education, referral and advocacy hub)
programs.cost_summary: 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Quiz and practitioner directory are free; Clarke's 12-chapter self-treatment course is described as free (no price on the course page). Rewiring Project membership starts at US$5.50/month (Community tier; ~$66/yr); professional tiers exist but prices are not posted; first month free. 2026 conference registration price not posted (member discount); pre-conference workshops +$126. 2023 virtual conference was reportedly $375 with CE/CME or $275 without (archived page, not re-verified). Therapy from directory practitioners is billed separately at private rates.
programs.mechanism_summary: ATNS calls these conditions "neuroplastic symptoms." The brain has learned a danger or alarm signal and keeps firing it, producing real pain or illness with no tissue damage behind it. Stress, unrecognised emotion and trauma (especially adverse childhood experiences) set it off. Personality habits such as perfectionism, people-pleasing and self-criticism keep it going, along with fear of the symptoms. The older PPDA protocol added Sarno-style psychodynamic ideas: symptoms express intolerable emotions somatically and distract from them. ATNS rejects Sarno's oxygen-deprivation hypothesis in favour of "learned neural pathways" that can be unlearned. It uses one mechanism for every condition ("Many Symptoms, One Brain"), from back pain to ME/CFS, long COVID, chronic Lyme, MCS, POTS and EDS, with a caveat to rule out structural disease first.

programs.mechanism_summary: The core model splits primary suffering (the raw sensation of pain or illness, possibly unchangeable) from secondary suffering (resistance, aversion, catastrophising, rumination, bodily bracing, held breath, and 'blocking' or 'drowning' styles). Secondary suffering is the modifiable target. Kindly, open mindful awareness, soft breathing, compassion and pacing reduce it. The model does not claim to explain disease causes. It accepts medical diagnoses and aims to change the person's relationship to symptoms rather than cure them. One transdiagnostic model is applied to all pain, illness and stress.

programs.cost_summary: Free or copay for eligible veterans in VHA; VA manuals and workbooks are free PDFs. US private practice about USD 100-250 per session, so about USD 1,200-3,000 for 12 sessions before insurance (estimate, 2026). Usually insurance-covered.
programs.mechanism_summary: Biopsychosocial model plus gate control/neuromatrix theory. Chronic pain is maintained by a cycle of inactivity, avoidance, deconditioning, depression and poor sleep. It is amplified by catastrophizing, low self-efficacy and operantly reinforced pain behaviours. Pain is treated as real, with nociceptive and tissue contributions, and as managed rather than cured. The goal is function and quality of life, not elimination of a brain-generated danger signal. The same transdiagnostic model is applied across pain diagnoses, with headache-specific (CBT-HA) and other condition variants.

programs.mechanism_summary: A trigger (usually a virus) starts the illness, and cognitive-behavioural perpetuating factors are said to maintain it. These are somatic illness attributions, fear that activity causes harm, low sense of control, focus on fatigue, avoidance or boom-bust activity patterns, physical deconditioning and sleep/circadian disruption, together forming a self-confirming vicious circle (Wessely 1989; Vercoulen 1998 Nijmegen model). GET specifically targets deconditioning and exercise intolerance. Post-exertional malaise is interpreted as deconditioning or expectation rather than a distinct physiology. The same logic is applied transdiagnostically to post-COVID fatigue and other persistent physical symptoms.

programs.mechanism_summary: The program treats these conditions as one nervous system "stuck, not broken" in a chronic stress/threat response. A trigger (infection, stress, overload) switches on an alarm that stays on. The resulting real symptoms are then read as danger, which keeps the loop going, with fear of symptoms as the key maintaining factor. A "stress threshold/bucket" (allostatic load) model has all stressors filling a single tank. Supporting language includes sympathetic overactivity, a non-resetting HPA axis, central sensitisation, vagal brain-immune signalling and neuroplastic reversibility. It is one mechanism for ME/CFS, long COVID, fibromyalgia and POTS; individualisation is through a proprietary assessment, not by disease.

programs.name: Cognitive Functional Therapy (CFT)
founders: Peter O'Sullivan (specialist musculoskeletal physiotherapist, Professor, Curtin University; director of Body Logic Physiotherapy and Evoolve)
JP Caneiro (physiotherapist, PhD, Associate Professor; co-director of Evoolve and Body Logic)
Key collaborators/co-developers (not founders): Peter Kent (Curtin; RESTORE lead; Evoolve technical support), Kieran O'Sullivan, Kjartan Vibe Fersum, Wim Dankaerts, Mary O'Keeffe, Anne Smith
programs.founded_year_range: 2005-2013 (estimate). Grew out of O'Sullivan's 2005 motor-control classification of low back pain into 'classification-based CFT'. The term first appears in PubMed-indexed titles in 2013 (Vibe Fersum RCT; Caneiro case report). Definitive description in Phys Ther 2018. The Evoolve training enterprise dates to about 2023-2024 (researcher-reported ABN and Wayback dates, not re-verified).
programs.cost_summary: Patients pay standard private physiotherapy fees, and Body Logic does not post prices. Typical Australian physio costs roughly AU$100-200 per session, so about 5-7 sessions comes to roughly AU$700-1,400 (about US$450-900) before rebates. This is an estimate. Clinician training through Evoolve (verified Oct 2026): the Tier 1 online course is US$330 for high-income countries, US$165 for middle-income and US$33 for low-income, plus tax, with student discounts. Masterclasses and later training tiers are priced separately. Some free courses and patient resources are offered. Evoolve describes itself as a social enterprise.
programs.mechanism_summary: CFT treats disabling low back pain as multidimensional and biopsychosocial. Pain persists through a self-reinforcing cycle with several parts: beliefs that the back is damaged or fragile; fear and catastrophising; low self-efficacy; protective movement behaviours such as bracing, breath-holding, guarded movement and avoidance; lifestyle factors such as inactivity, poor sleep and stress; and social context. Peripheral and central sensitisation are acknowledged as possible contributors, and pathology is screened for, not denied. The earlier version stressed maladaptive motor-control patterns; that rigid classification was later de-emphasised. In RESTORE, changes in self-efficacy, fear, catastrophising and early pain mediated up to about 61-62% of the treatment effect. The framework is individualised per person, not per diagnosis. It is applied mainly to musculoskeletal pain and makes no claims for ME/CFS, POTS, MCS or similar syndromes.

founders: Barry McDonagh (Irish author; BA UCD, HDip Psychology Open University; not a licensed clinician; app developer BMD Publishing Ltd)
Dr Claire Weekes (1903-1990; Australian physician/GP; BSc 1926, DSc 1930 Sydney, MB 1945; MBE 1978)

programs.cost_summary: DARE app has a free tier. US iOS premium is $9.99-12.99/mo or $53.99-69.99/yr, and one-off 'Rapid Relief' audio packs cost $16.99. programs.mechanism_summary: Weekes held that a stressor sensitizes the nervous system, so fear and bodily sensations come faster and stronger than normal. "Second fear" (fear of the first fear, plus "what if" thinking and struggle) re-sensitizes the system and keeps the cycle going. Recovery comes from changing one's reaction to the sensations (face, accept, float, let time pass), which lets the system self-desensitize; finding the original cause is not needed. DARE restates this in modern terms: resisting, avoiding and seeking safety from a harmless fight-or-flight response maintains anxiety, and repeatedly allowing and even inviting the sensations "retrains" the nervous system. Both use one transdiagnostic model, with no differentiation by medical syndrome.

Benign stimuli (odours, foods, EMFs, exertion, body sensations) are then misread as dangers, producing real symptoms via central sensitisation and a chronic stress response, sustained by hypervigilance and avoidance. Recovery is framed as rewiring this circuitry through daily practice that interrupts threat patterns and rehearses elevated positive states. The same mechanism applies to every condition; only the personal triggers differ.

Chronic pain is framed as amplified by stress, emotions and unresolved trauma. All targets share the same mechanism and sequence. Critics accept the exposure and cognitive components as plausible but dispute that tapping is a specific active ingredient.

programs.name: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
founders: Francine Shapiro, PhD (1948-2019; PhD 1988, Professional School of Psychological Studies, San Diego, unaccredited and now defunct; later Senior Research Fellow, Mental Research Institute, Palo Alto)
EMDR Institute (emdr.com; created 1990, incorporated 1993)

programs.founded_year_range: 1987-1995 (1987: Shapiro's observation; 1989: first published as EMD; 1990: EMDR Institute; 1991: renamed EMDR; 1993: Institute incorporated; 1995: training restrictions lifted, EMDRIA founded; 2014: 'EMDR therapy'), per emdr.com history page
programs.cost_summary: No central price. Background estimate (not verified this session): US sessions about US$100-250 each, with 6-15 sessions typical, so roughly US$1,000-3,000 per course. EMDRIA says training prices vary by site. Clinician basic training about US$1,500-2,500 (EMDRIA minimum is 20 h instruction + 20 h practicum + 10 h consultation). Free on the NHS for PTSD.
programs.mechanism_summary: Shapiro's Adaptive Information Processing (AIP) model holds that symptoms come from inadequately processed adverse memories, stored with their original images, emotions, body sensations and negative beliefs. Bilateral stimulation during recall is said to engage innate processing that integrates these memories adaptively. Research accounts instead propose working-memory taxing that reduces vividness and leads to reconsolidation, or plain exposure/extinction. For chronic pain, 'pain memories' (pre-amputation pain, injuries, medical trauma) and trauma-linked threat sensitization are proposed to maintain pain. Processing these memories and the current pain sensation is proposed to reduce pain and distress. The model is transdiagnostic in principle, but the pain applications target mainly trauma-exposed or highly distressed patients.

programs.founded_year_range: 2008-2012. Precursor trials ran 2006-2011 (affective self-awareness, Hsu 2010). The NIAMS R01 AR057808 trial first called it 'Emotional Exposure Therapy'. Manual v2 used the EAET name by Sept 2012. The name first appeared in a paper in 2016 (Burger).

programs.mechanism_summary: EAET holds that the brain generates or amplifies primary/centralized pain and other somatic symptoms. Lifetime trauma, adversity and interpersonal or intrapsychic conflict sensitize a brain "danger/alarm" system. Avoidance of primary emotions ("affect phobia") keeps that system active: chiefly anger tied to agency and assertion, plus guilt, grief and longing tied to attachment. Symptoms are expected to resolve through three processes. Patients re-attribute pain to the brain and emotion. They undergo experiential exposure to the avoided emotions, which works as a corrective emotional experience or "memory reconsolidation". They practise adaptive assertive and connecting expression in real relationships. One mechanism is applied across fibromyalgia, IBS, pelvic pain, MUS/SSD, musculoskeletal pain and headache. Patients with high trauma or conflict loads are expected to be the best candidates.

The class also uses relaxation and self-soothing to lower arousal, and positive expectancy and self-efficacy to counter nocebo. founders: David S. Butler (physiotherapist, EdD; founder/director of NOI, early 1990s)

programs.mechanism_summary: Pain is a protective output the brain constructs when it evaluates credible evidence of danger. It is not a measure of tissue damage. In persistent pain, a bioplastic nervous system becomes sensitised and overprotective: peripheral and central sensitisation, altered cortical body maps, and immune and endocrine protective responses. Pain is also cued by learned contexts. Threatening beliefs, catastrophizing and fear of movement keep the system sensitive. The Protectometer frames pain as the balance of 'Danger in Me' versus 'Safety in Me' cues. Reconceptualising pain (conceptual change) is the proposed active ingredient, combined with graded exposure. The scope is pain; it does not claim a single brain disorder spanning ME/CFS, MCS or POTS.

programs.mechanism_summary: Pain and dysfunction are attributed to learned, inefficient or protective habitual action organised by the person's "self-image" (movement, sensation, feeling, thought), such as excess effort, co-contraction and guarding. Slow, small, effortless, varied movements done with attention to differences are meant to allow sensorimotor relearning: a refined body schema, better interoceptive awareness and less protective threat behaviour. Modern proponents frame this as neuroplasticity. The method has no disease-specific mechanisms and makes no claims about ME/CFS, POTS, MCS or similar illnesses.

GMI activates premotor networks first, then motor networks, then a visual illusion of normal movement. Each step stays below the threshold that triggers protective pain, which unpairs movement from pain. The 2005 order-dependence trial is cited as support. Moseley states that the mechanism is unclear.

The mechanism has not been tested in any trial (no imaging or conditioning measures).

programs.mechanism_summary: IBS and related disorders are framed as disorders of gut-brain interaction, involving visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility and gut-focused anxiety or hypervigilance. Hypnotic suggestion and imagery are proposed to modulate visceral afferent processing from the top down. Evidence for this: rectal sensitivity normalised in Manchester data (Lea 2003), and anterior-insula responses to distension were attenuated in responders to both hypnosis and education, with posterior-insula attenuation specific to hypnosis responders (Lowen 2013). Hypnosis is also thought to reduce the gastrocolonic response (Simren 2004), somatization and distress (Palsson 2002), and catastrophizing (Gonsalkorale 2004). Immune effects are speculative, from UC work. The mechanism is not settled: UNC and paediatric studies found no change in rectal thresholds. The approach is organ-directed, with scripts tailored to colon, oesophagus or upper GI, and it makes no cross-syndrome claims.

programs.mechanism_summary: Sensory-Motor Amnesia: repeated stress (injury, surgery, repetitive tasks, emotional stress) produces habituated, involuntary muscle contraction that the sensorimotor cortex can no longer sense or release. The patterns follow three stress reflexes: Red Light (flexor/withdrawal), Green Light (extensor/action) and Trauma (asymmetric guarding). The tight muscles compress joints and nerves, causing pain, stiffness and the posture usually blamed on aging. Voluntary pandiculation (contract, slow release, rest) is said to restore central control and reset resting tone. This is a learned sensorimotor-habit model, not a central-sensitisation model.

Healing comes from unblending from protectors, accessing Self, then witnessing and unburdening exiles. One model is applied across all conditions, and IFS offers no pain-neuroscience or central-sensitisation model of its own.

programs.mechanism_summary: Painful early attachment experiences leave complex mixed feelings (rage, guilt about rage, grief) that are kept out of awareness. When current situations re-evoke them, unconscious anxiety and defenses (including somatisation and self-attack) produce symptoms; this is Malan's triangle of conflict. Unconscious anxiety is said to discharge through distinct bodily pathways, and each pathway maps onto a symptom class: striated muscle (musculoskeletal pain, tension headache), smooth muscle/autonomic (IBS, migraine, bladder), cognitive-perceptual disruption (dizziness, blurred vision, dissociation) and motor conversion (FND, functional seizures). The cause is a single unified one, but the anxiety pathway determines technique (high-pressure versus the graded format). Abbass and Schubiner add a neuroscience gloss (psychophysiologic disorders, brain-generated danger signals). ME/CFS, long COVID, MCS and EHS are not addressed.

Repeated practice of a proprietary interrupt technique is meant to rewire these pathways through neuroplasticity. The site calls ME/CFS a physical illness and LP 'neuro-physiological', not psychological. The same model is applied to every condition.

A physician triage separates primary pain from structural pain (white-paper figures: 70% primary only, 26% mixed, 4% structural). The same model is applied to every listed condition, including POTS, CFS, IBS, hives and tinnitus.

programs.mechanism_summary: After recovery from depression, mild dysphoria can reactivate depressogenic thinking (cognitive reactivity). MBCT trains decentering and metacognitive awareness ("thoughts are not facts") and a "being mode", so people notice early warning signs and disengage. The theoretical basis is Teasdale's ICS model. MBCT claims no central neurological or autonomic cause of somatic illness. Adaptations for pain and health anxiety apply the same reactivity model to aversive sensations.

Non-judgmental, present-moment awareness is taught to "uncouple" the sensory side of pain and symptoms from cognitive and emotional elaboration, and to replace stress "reaction" with "response," which the program presents as reducing sympathetic and HPA load. Later research models add attention regulation, interoception, emotion regulation and changes in self-perspective.

programs.mechanism_summary: The original model was 'hypothalamitis', and the program now calls it the 'Prolonged Activation State' (PAS). In this model, feelings that arise from present-day interactions are repeatedly overridden or left unanswered, and each new situation adds fresh activation. The hypothalamus, described on the site as the coordinating centre for the nervous, endocrine and immune systems, is said to stay 'on' as a result, producing fatigue, pain, brain fog, sensitivities and immune or allergy-type ('MCAS-type') symptoms. An infection can start the process, but PAS is explicitly 'not the residue of that event' and is not framed as past trauma or repressed emotion. Symptoms are treated as messages that call for a response. One model covers all of the conditions the program claims to treat.

programs.name: Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE)
founders: Eric L. Garland, PhD, LCSW (formerly University of Utah; now UC San Diego Dept. of Psychiatry / Sanford Institute)
programs.founded_year_range: 2007-2008. The first pilot RCT ran in 2008 (Garland et al. 2010, J Psychoactive Drugs). The name MORE was in print by 2012, and the NASW Press manual was published in 2013.
programs.cost_summary: Patients: no published price. MORE is billed as group/individual psychotherapy or group medical visits where offered (e.g. Essentia Health since 2021), and is free in trials. Clinicians: online certification course lists at USD 895, on sale at USD 716 (institute.moretherapy.com, Oct 2026). It is a one-time payment for annual membership and includes 12 self-paced modules (~10 h), monthly live sessions, a free annual subscription to the companion app and up to 10 CE hours (NAADAC/NASW-Utah). Earlier 2-day live trainings cost USD 500. Guilford manual published 2024.
programs.mechanism_summary: MORE uses a "downward spiral" allostatic model in which chronic pain, negative affect and opioid use reinforce one another. Opioid exposure produces hedonic dysregulation: drug cues gain salience (attentional bias, cue-reactivity, craving) while natural rewards lose value (anhedonia). This combines with attentional bias toward pain and catastrophizing appraisals. Treatment targets the attention–appraisal–reward interface with three skills. Mindfulness reinterprets pain as neutral sensations and interrupts automatic habits. Reappraisal reduces catastrophizing. Savoring restores natural-reward responsiveness. Proposed biomarkers include HRV during meditation (Am Psychol 2020), frontal-midline theta (Neuropsychopharmacology 2021) and LPP/P300 reward responses (Sci Adv 2019). The model stays within mainstream neuroscience and is used alongside medication; it does not claim pain is purely brain-generated.

Hypnosis (relaxation, focused attention, gut-directed imagery and suggestion) is said to calm gut signalling directly, while CBT-informed lessons target the thoughts and behaviours around symptoms. The model is disorder-specific (IBS/DGBI), not a transdiagnostic one-illness model.

programs.mechanism_summary: The shared premise is that symptoms reflect dysregulated brain oscillations, arousal or network dynamics. Real-time EEG feedback trains the brain by operant conditioning toward more regulated patterns, which then persist through plasticity. Classic and Othmer ILF models map conditions onto over- or under-arousal and instability: SMR/alpha up-training and theta/high-beta inhibit for pain and sleep, alpha-theta for trauma. qEEG/LORETA models normalise z-score deviations from a database. Research protocols for fibromyalgia target amygdala/limbic or pgACC-S1 networks (central sensitisation). NeurOptimal rejects diagnosis-specific protocols: it interrupts music at EEG 'turbulence' so the brain 'self-organises'. Muse trains meditation attention. Critics attribute much of the benefit to placebo and psychosocial factors.

Fibromyalgia, IBS, ME/CFS, migraine and chronic pain are seen as overlapping "functional disorders," possibly "ONE condition with different aspects." Core FND symptoms are distinguished from these associated ones, and comorbid organic disease is acknowledged.

Reappraising sensations as safe through somatic tracking and evidence-gathering is meant to produce safety learning or extinction. The developers' trial reported matching fMRI changes: reduced aMCC/aPFC responses to evoked back pain vs placebo, reduced anterior insula responses vs usual care, and increased aPFC/anterior insula-S1 resting connectivity. A single model covers all neuroplastic symptoms. Structural pain is distinguished from neuroplastic pain, and "mixed" pain is treated as only partly reducible.

The model is biopsychosocial: predisposing factors, precipitating triggers, and perpetuating factors (attention, beliefs, habitual movement patterns, reinforcement, deconditioning). programs.mechanism_summary: The model is a phylogenetically ordered three-tier autonomic hierarchy. The ventral vagal 'social engagement' state supports safety and connection; sympathetic mobilisation (fight/flight) comes next; dorsal vagal immobilisation (shutdown, dissociation, collapse) is last. 'Neuroception' is an unconscious detection of safety or threat; when it is faulty after trauma or chronic threat, it keeps people stuck in defensive states. Co-regulation through face, voice and prosody restores ventral state. Chronic pain, functional GI disorders, fatigue, anxiety and depression are read as expressions of sympathetic- or dorsal-dominant defensive states (e.g., Kolacz & Porges 2018). One transdiagnostic mechanism covers all of them, and conditions differ by state rather than disease.

Benign cues then retrigger it. The proposed fix is repeated self-directed neuroplasticity training plus somatic regulation. One model is applied to all conditions.

programs.mechanism_summary: Chronic or repeated activation of Cannon's fight-or-flight response (sympathetic arousal, stress hormones) is held to cause or worsen many conditions. The relaxation response is an innate counter-state: lower metabolism, heart rate, breathing rate and BP, and reduced noradrenergic responsiveness. Two elements elicit it: a repetitive mental focus and passive disregard of intruding thoughts. Later work added genomic claims, from small, preliminary studies, that NF-kB inflammatory genes are downregulated and energy-metabolism genes upregulated, and the role of belief ("remembered wellness"). The 3RP resiliency model combines RR physiology with stress awareness, cognitive appraisal, positive psychology and lifestyle. Stress is framed as an aggravator across many diseases, including organic ones, not as the single cause of a unified syndrome.

Trait hypnotizability, screened in-app with a remote Hypnotic Induction Profile, predicts benefit. There is no disease-specific theory of chronic illness: symptoms are treated as states that attention and suggestion can modulate.

programs.mechanism_summary: Based on Polyvagal Theory. "Neuroception" of threat is said to lock the autonomic nervous system into sympathetic or dorsal-vagal defense, and with it the cranial-nerve "social engagement system," which includes the middle-ear muscles and vagal control of the heart. This produces auditory hypersensitivity, poor social engagement, anxiety, trauma symptoms and bodily symptoms. Music filtered to emphasize the frequencies of human prosody is claimed to act as a "neural exercise" for the middle-ear muscles, raising ventral-vagal tone (RSA) and making felt safety accessible. One mechanism is used for every condition; only pacing and pathway are titrated.

programs.mechanism_summary: Unconscious repressed emotion, chiefly rage from childhood, personality (perfectionism, "goodism") and life pressures, threatens to reach awareness. The brain creates physical symptoms as a distraction (defence). Sarno's original physiology: the brain uses the autonomic nervous system to cause mild, harmless ischaemia in muscles, nerves and tendons. This was never demonstrated. The "symptom imperative": if a symptom is treated physically, the brain substitutes another, producing "TMS equivalents" (IBS, headache, GERD, tinnitus, skin, anxiety/depression). Fear of structural diagnoses perpetuates the pain. The cure is knowledge: accepting the psychological diagnosis removes the distraction's purpose. Successors (Schubiner, Gordon) recast it as neuroplastic/brain-generated pain and threat conditioning.

programs.mechanism_summary: Chronic physical and mental symptoms are said to be adaptations of an autonomic nervous system dysregulated by stored, incomplete survival responses (fight/flight/freeze) arising from developmental or attachment trauma, injury, surgery, infection or chronic stress. The nervous system "governs all other systems," so dysregulation spreads to immune, endocrine and digestive function; freeze/dorsal-vagal shutdown is linked to autoimmunity. Healing means growing nervous-system "capacity" (the window of tolerance) bottom-up through interoceptive and sensorimotor learning (neuroplasticity, infant-like attunement), not top-down cognition. "Fluid/chemical trauma" from toxins is a further sub-layer, for which detox adjuncts are recommended.

programs.mechanism_summary: Trauma symptoms are attributed to thwarted, incomplete defensive responses (fight, flight, freeze). These leave 'survival energy' and autonomic activation bound in the nervous system, producing sympathetic hyperarousal and dorsal-vagal shutdown or dissociation (polyvagal framing). Payne, Levine and Crane-Godreau (2015) recast this as dysregulation of a subcortical 'core response network' of autonomic, limbic, motor and arousal systems. Persisting activation is proposed to drive somatic symptoms such as chronic pain, migraine, fibromyalgia and fatigue. The model is a single transdiagnostic mechanism; it is differentiated only by trauma type (shock vs developmental) and autonomic state, not by diagnosis.

Collaborators later reframed the model in predictive-processing terms.

CES (Alpha-Stim, Fisher Wallace) delivers ear or temple alternating microcurrent. It is claimed to shift EEG toward alpha, lower arousal, and modulate neurotransmitters and the autonomic state. Pain/fibromyalgia: high-frequency M1 stimulation engages descending inhibitory/opioid pathways and restores intracortical inhibition, countering central sensitisation. programs.mechanism_summary: Tremoring is presented as an innate mammalian reflex that discharges stress or trauma energy once a threat has passed. Adults suppress it, so the stress response stays incomplete and is held as chronic muscle tension, especially in the psoas. Deliberately fatiguing the leg and psoas muscles and then allowing 'neurogenic tremors' is said to let the nervous system self-regulate back toward parasympathetic balance, with no need for verbal processing or belief. The same model applies to all conditions. Polyvagal framing was added later. Critics read the tremor as ordinary fatigue tremor, with benefits coming from relaxation and expectancy.

One mechanism is applied to pain, IBS, bladder symptoms, fatigue, POTS, anxiety and depression. Patients are differentiated mainly by whether their symptoms are primary or secondary (structural). Cefaly stimulates supraorbital/supratrochlear trigeminal branches to desensitize the trigeminal system. Relivion (and Neurolief's Proliv Rx for depression) stimulates occipital and trigeminal branches together, targeting the trigemino-cervical complex and brainstem. programs.mechanism_summary: This is a hormesis/self-regulation model rather than a disease model. Cyclic hyperventilation followed by breath retention causes respiratory alkalosis and intermittent hypoxia, which produces a large epinephrine surge. In an acute endotoxin challenge, that surge raised IL-10 and suppressed TNF-a/IL-6/IL-8 (Kox 2014, PNAS). Graded cold exposure is said to train vascular, brown-fat and stress resilience, and 'mindset/commitment' is said to give top-down ('brain over body') control of autonomic and immune function. Marketing adds uncited vagal, cortisol and 'alkalizing' claims. The core mechanism is deliberate acute sympathetic activation, which is unusual in this survey. There are no condition-specific models, only contraindications.

programs.name: Wise-Anderson Protocol / 'A Headache in the Pelvis' (Stanford Protocol)
founders: David Wise, PhD (licensed California psychologist; 8 years as visiting research scholar in Stanford Urology; former CP/CPPS patient; National Center for Pelvic Pain Research; inventor of the internal wand, New Pelvic Pain Technologies)
Rodney U. Anderson, MD, FACS (Professor Emeritus of Urology, Stanford)
programs.founded_year_range: 1995-2003. Wise and Anderson began collaborating in the mid-1990s, and their 2018 meta-analysis dates the 'new paradigm' to 1995. The protocol was developed over about 8 years at Stanford. The book's first edition was self-published in 2003, and the 6-day clinics ran from the mid-2000s.
delivery: device (internal trigger point wand, external Genie)
programs.cost_summary: No prices on the site ('contact for eligibility and cost'). A single 2014 patient-forum report put the 6-day clinic at about USD 3,000-4,000, excluding travel; the yearlong audio course was included. This figure is unverified and likely out of date, and the current format is 2-day. Book about USD 20-30. Prices for the wand and the 60-day home program are not published. The clinic is self-pay; the pre-clinic urology evaluation may be billed to insurance.
programs.mechanism_summary: The protocol frames CP/CPPS and related pelvic pain as a 'psychoneuromuscular' disorder rather than prostate infection: a 'headache in the pelvis.' Anxiety, stress or an initial injury leads to chronic protective guarding of the pelvic floor muscles. The guarding produces myofascial trigger points, shortened and ischaemic tissue, nerve irritation and referred pain. Pain then raises anxiety and catastrophizing, which drive further guarding (a tension-anxiety-pain cycle sustained by autonomic arousal). One mechanism is applied across pelvic syndromes in both sexes, but only to patients with the pelvic-floor-tenderness phenotype. It is a peripheral-plus-central loop in which muscle and tissue change is the pain generator, not a purely 'brain-generated pain' model.

founders: No single founder (umbrella practice)

Lineage: T. Krishnamacharya, B.K.S. Iyengar, T.K.V. Desikachar

programs.founded_year_range: 1989 for IAYT (secondary sources; iayt.org not reachable). Therapeutic postural yoga dates to the 1920s–40s (Kaivalyadhama 1924; Iyengar remedial yoga from about 1940). C-IAYT credential about 2016 (approx.); TCTSY 2002.
